claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the interplay between valence electron count and lattice disorder.
Increasing the titanium fraction increases the alloy's valence electron count.
Increasing titanium content enhances electron-phonon coupling.
A modest increase in titanium content raises Tc when a single-phase disordered solid solution is preserved.
Increasing titanium content may increase the upper critical field Hc2.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase, disordered, near-equiatomic solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
Titanium content can be varied while preserving a single-phase disordered solid solution.
The relevant superconducting regime is below approximately 10 K.
Weak-coupling BCS theory is applicable to the proposed alloy.
Lattice disorder and local bonding variations modulate the density of states near the Fermi level.
Changing valence electron count alters the density of states and electron-phonon coupling strength.
The balance between carrier concentration and disorder-induced localization governs superconducting properties in a highly disordered lattice.
Configurational entropy can sustain a uniform solid solution.
Valence electron count can be a principal correlate of Tc in a disordered HEA superconductor family.
Compositional disorder can either suppress or enhance superconductivity, depending on the regime.
The baseline alloy has lower titanium content, lower valence electron count, and lower Tc than an optimal modified composition.
The proposed VEC-disorder mechanism applies only to single-phase solid-solution HEAs.
Phase separation or intermetallic precipitation invalidates or obscures the proposed relationship between VEC, disorder, and superconductivity.
A phase-pure titanium-composition series processed identically can test whether Tc and Hc2 rise systematically relative to the starting alloy.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the mechanism does not apply after phase separation or intermetallic precipitation, whereas the falsification rule treats occurrence of those out-of-boundary states as falsifying the mechanism rather than making the test uninterpretable.
